title: Transverse Cold Rolling-Induced Microstructural Modification and Mechanical and Electrochemical Responses of UNS S32304 Lean Duplex Stainless Steel
abstract: Abstract This study provides a critical assessment of transverse cold rolling as an alternative deformation route for controlling anisotropy in UNS S32304 lean duplex stainless steel by correlating microstructural evolution with mechanical, corrosion, and tribological responses. Although transverse cold rolling up to 50% thickness reduction did not fully randomize the microstructure or suppress the anisotropy inherited from prior cold rolling, it revealed distinct section-dependent deformation behavior and pronounced strain hardening. This leads to a substantial increase in ultimate tensile strength independent of loading orientation and without inducing martensitic transformation. Notably, the material preserved its high corrosion resistance, showing low susceptibility to intergranular corrosion despite the imposed plastic strain. However, pitting occurred in the top section for all treatments in 3.5% NaCl, with the lowest pitting potential for the hot-rolled condition. Conversely, tribological performance remained limited, with inferior wear resistance in distilled water compared to mineral oil. These results demonstrate that, while transverse cold rolling enhances strength without compromising corrosion resistance, it is not an effective standalone strategy for anisotropy reduction or tribological improvement at moderate deformation levels, thereby establishing clear boundaries for its applicability and providing guidance for the design of alternative processing routes.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The growing demand for high-performance materials in sectors such as aerospace, automotive, chemical processing, and oil and gas has stimulated the development of metallic alloys that combine enhanced mechanical properties, corrosion resistance in aggressive environments, and good formability (Ref  1 ). Among commercially available metallic alloys, duplex stainless steels (DSSs) are particularly attractive for applications requiring an optimized balance between high mechanical strength and excellent corrosion resistance (Ref  2 ,  3 ,  4 - 5 ). These steels are termed duplex because their microstructure consists of approximately equal proportions of austenite ( γ ) and ferrite ( α ). Such a biphasic structure provides superior mechanical strength and enhanced corrosion resistance compared with conventional austenitic stainless steels.

Warm and hot-rolled DSSs commonly exhibit a pronounced banded microstructure, characterized by a strong alignment between austenite and ferrite (Ref  6 ,  7 - 8 ). Under these conditions, austenite grains nucleating from the ferrite matrix tend to adopt specific crystallographic orientation relationships with the parent phase (Ref  9 ,  10 ) leading to the development of phase-transformation textures and, consequently, pronounced anisotropic behavior. Following cold rolling, DSSs are commonly tempered to relieve stress (Ref  11 ,  12 ) which partially randomizes the orientation of both phases. When subsequently cold rolled in the same direction as the original hot rolling pass, new deformation textures develop in austenite and ferrite through the characteristic crystallographic rotation mechanisms of ferrite and austenite structures. As a result, the material usually exhibits marked plastic anisotropy. Upon annealing, recrystallization further modifies the texture but does not necessarily eliminate anisotropy. Only DSSs that are hot-rolled and subsequently subjected to optimized heat treatments tend to produce isotropic properties; all other processing routes typically retain significant anisotropy. However, if cold rolling is performed in a direction transverse to the banding imposed by cold rolling, the resulting textures, diffusional interactions, and deformation modes may differ substantially (Ref  13 ).

Comparable behavior has been reported in niobium-containing austenitic stainless steels, where niobium precipitation during cold rolling suppresses recrystallization in the austenitic field (Ref  14 ). Continued rolling at decreasing temperatures therefore leads to the development of a pronounced banded microstructure. Both niobium-stabilized austenitic stainless steels and DSSs frequently exhibit strong anisotropy in Charpy impact toughness, depending on notch orientation. These similarities suggest that rolling DSSs in a direction transverse to the banding may disrupt phase alignment, potentially promoting more homogeneous microstructural evolution and mechanical response after deformation and recrystallization owing to more uniform diffusional and deformation interactions between phases.

Starting from a microstructure that has undergone only cold rolling, thus still exhibiting a degree of alignment, offers a controlled initial condition to investigate how accommodation between the phases affects properties. The banded morphology influences lattice rotation, slip activity, and phase interactions during transverse cold rolling, and the resulting microstructural changes can significantly affect ductility, toughness, strength, and corrosion behavior, depending on the direction analyzed. Therefore, it is essential to determine whether cold rolling in this transverse direction modifies the banded morphology, alters grain orientations and texture evolution, and reduces the anisotropy typically observed in DSSs.

The literature consistently shows that the banded morphology promotes anisotropic mechanical and alters corrosion properties in DSSs. However, most studies have examined cold rolling along the same direction as cold rolling, which preserves the banded structure (Ref  15 ,  16 ,  17 - 18 ). In contrast, the effects of non-conventional rolling paths, such as transverse or cross cold rolling, remain largely unexplored, particularly for DSSs. Most studies have focused on austenitic stainless steels (Ref  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 - 24 ), while only a limited number of studies extend these concepts to other classes of metallic materials (Ref  6 ,  25 ,  26 - 27 ).

DSSs may become susceptible to sensitization when exposed to specific thermal conditions that promote the precipitation of chromium-rich secondary phases. During thermal exposure in the approximate temperature range of 300-1000 °C, such as during welding or thermal aging, phases including σ (sigma), chromium carbides (Cr 23 C 6 ), nitrides, and Cr-rich α′ can form in the microstructure. The precipitation of these phases leads to local depletion of chromium and molybdenum in the surrounding matrix, which compromises the passive film stability and increases susceptibility to intergranular corrosion. Among these transformations, the formation and growth of the σ phase at temperatures above ~ 600 °C is often reported as the main mechanism responsible for sensitization and degradation of corrosion resistance in DSSs. The kinetics of these precipitation reactions depend strongly on temperature, exposure time, and alloy composition, particularly the contents of Cr and Mo that promote σ-phase formation. As a result, prolonged thermal exposure or improper thermal cycles can significantly increase the degree of sensitization (DOS) and reduce the corrosion resistance of duplex stainless steels (Ref  28 ). Furthermore, microstructural imbalances, such as a fully ferritic structure produced by rapid solidification processes or inadequate heat treatment, can also negatively affect corrosion resistance and repassivation behavior of DSSs, reinforcing the importance of maintaining a balanced ferrite–austenite microstructure to avoid degradation phenomena (Ref  29 ). Although DL-EPR testing was initially developed for evaluating sensitization in austenitic stainless steels, it has also been widely applied to duplex stainless steels to detect chromium-depleted regions associated with the precipitation of deleterious phases. Therefore, double-loop electrochemical potentiokinetic reactivation (DL-EPR) testing provides a useful electrochemical approach to evaluate the presence of chromium-depleted regions and quantify the degree of sensitization in duplex stainless steels.

In this context, the present study explores transverse cold rolling as a non-conventional deformation route for duplex stainless steels, aiming to clarify its influence on microstructural evolution and anisotropy. Using UNS S32304 lean duplex stainless steel in the hot-rolled condition as a model system, this work examines whether deformation applied transverse to the inherited banded morphology can disrupt phase alignment, alter phase configurations, and thereby affect the response of the material. The study further investigates whether such microstructural changes can provide a favorable balance between mechanical strength and corrosion resistance without the need for subsequent heat treatment. To this end, the effects of transverse cold rolling up to 50% thickness reduction on the microstructure and on the mechanical, corrosion, and tribological behavior of UNS S32304 steel are evaluated. By assessing both the potential and the limitations of this approach, the present work aims to delineate the practical applicability of transverse cold rolling for anisotropy control in duplex stainless steels.

sections.heading: Chemical Characterization
paragraphs:
A 12-mm-thick plate of UNS S32304 duplex stainless steel, supplied by Aperam South America in the industrially processed hot-rolled and annealed condition, was the base material for this investigation. Its chemical composition, presented in Table  1 , was determined using complementary analytical techniques. Spark optical emission spectrometry (S-OES) was performed using SPECTROMAXx equipment to quantify the primary alloying elements. Interstitial elements were measured via inert gas fusion: nitrogen and oxygen contents were determined by thermal conductivity detection using a Leco ONH-836 analyzer, while carbon and sulfur were analyzed by infrared detection employing a Leco CS-844 analyzer. In addition, energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was performed to complement the compositional analysis and provide local chemical characterization.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic Calculation of Phases
paragraphs: Computational thermodynamic calculations were performed using the CALPHAD method in Thermo-Calc software. A commercial database for ferrous alloys (TCFE7) was utilized, which includes Fe-Cr-Ni-Mn-Mo-Si-C and all their respective binaries, covering a wide range of chemical composition (see Table  1 ) and temperature. The result was used to determine the temperature at which both phases are present in the alloy in the similar amount to better plan the cold rolling passes.

sections.heading: Non-Conventional Processing Route
paragraphs: The complete processing sequence is illustrated in Figure  1 . The starting material was a 12-mm-thick industrial hot-rolled and annealed UNS S32304 plate, hereafter referred to as IHR. To intentionally accentuate microstructural anisotropy, this plate was hot-rolled at 1050 °C with a 50% thickness reduction via multiple passes, maintaining the original industrial rolling direction. This produced a 6-mm-thick laboratory hot-rolled (HR) plate with an enhanced banded phase morphology. Without an intermediate stress-relief heat treatment, a section of the HR plate was directly subjected to transverse cold rolling (CR). This section was cut and oriented such that its hot rolling direction was perpendicular to the subsequent cold rolling direction. Transverse cold rolling was then performed at room temperature in multiple passes to a final 50% thickness reduction, resulting in an approximate final thickness of 3 mm. The analyzed sections are color-coded in Fig.  1 . The longitudinal section (LS, blue) of the HR condition corresponds to the transverse section (TS, blue) after cold rolling, while the HR transverse section (TS, yellow) becomes the longitudinal section (LS, yellow) post-deformation. Fig. 1 Schematic representation of the transversal cold rolling applied to UNS S32304 steel

sections.heading: Structural Characterization
paragraphs: The phases present in both HR and CR conditions for longitudinal and transversal sections of the UNS S32304 steel were identified by high-energy synchrotron x-ray diffraction (SXRD) experiments conducted at the P07 beamline of Petra III, located at the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY) in Hamburg, Germany. A fixed energy of 102.85 keV, corresponding to an x-ray wavelength of 0.120549 Å was employed for structural characterization of the steel.

The LS and TS of the UNS S32304 steel under hot-rolled and cold rolled conditions were examined using a JEOL JSM-7100FT field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM) in backscattering electron mode (BSE) at the Brazilian Center for Research in Physics in Rio de Janeiro (CBPF), Brazil. Moreover, elemental maps were obtained by Energy Dispersive x-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) in the TS of the CR condition using an Oxford Instruments EDS detector coupled to FESEM. Samples preparation involved grinding with SiC abrasive papers (220 to 2500 grit), polishing with 0.3  μ m alumina suspension, and final etching using a modified Kalling’s reagent (1.0 g CuCl 2  / 20 mg HCl/20 mg ethanol) by immersion for 3-5 seconds (Ref  30 ).

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out on both HR and CR conditions of the UNS S32304 steel, in longitudinal and transversal sections, at room temperature using an Instron 5900R testing machine, under a strain rate of 1.0 × 10 −3  s −1 . Three specimens from all sections and processing conditions were machined according to the dimensions shown in Fig.  2 . The yield strength ( σ ys ), ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and fracture strain ( ε ) were determined using the Instron Bluehill software. To evaluate the statistical significance, a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test at  α  = 0.01 was performed. Identical letters indicate no statistically significant difference. Fig. 2 Schematic representation of the sample used for uniaxial tensile testing of UNS S32304 steel

Vickers microhardness tests were performed on both HR and CR conditions of the UNS S32304 steel, in longitudinal and transversal sections, using a Shimadzu HMV-G 20ST microhardness tester with a Vickers indenter applying a 500-gf load for 15 s on polished sample surfaces. Ten indentations were made in each condition, with a minimum spacing of at least three times the diagonal length of the indentation. To evaluate the statistical significance, a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test at  α  = 0.01 was performed. Identical letters indicate no statistically significant difference.

sections.heading: Electrochemical Experiments
paragraphs: Electrochemical tests were performed in triplicate on the IHR, HR, and CR UNS S32304 conditions, examining top section. A conventional three-electrode cell was employed, utilizing the stainless steel sample as the working electrode (0.3 cm 2  exposed area), a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference, and a platinum mesh as the counter electrode. All measurements were conducted using a Gamry 600 + potentiostat. Prior to testing, the working electrodes were mechanically abraded with SiC abrasive paper up to 1200 grit. The electrolyte was naturally aerated, 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution prepared from high-purity reagents (> 99%) and deionized water. After the open-circuit potential (OCP) stabilized for one hour, cyclic potentiodynamic polarization scans were initiated. The potential was then scanned anodically from − 250 mV versus OCP at a rate of 1.0 mV s −1  until an anodic current density of 10 mA cm −2  was reached, followed by a reverse scan to the OCP at the same rate.

The susceptibility to intergranular corrosion was evaluated using the double-loop electrochemical potentiokinetic reactivation (DL-EPR) test, according to the ISO 12732 standard (Ref  31 ) Tests were performed in a deaerated solution of 0.5 mol L −1  H 2 SO 4  + 0.01 mol L −1  KSCN + 0.5 mol L −1  NaCl. After a 15-minute immersion at OCP, the potential was scanned anodically at 6.0 V h −1  (1.67 mV s −1 ) to + 300 mV SCE  and then reversed to the initial OCP. The activation current ( Iₐ ) and reactivation current ( Iᵣ ) peaks were recorded, and the degree of sensitization (DOS) was calculated as ( Iᵣ / Iₐ ) × 100%. Based on the standard, a DOS < 1% indicates an unsensitized microstructure, 1-5% indicates light sensitization, and > 5% indicates significant sensitization.

sections.heading: Tribological Experiments
paragraphs: Pin-on-disk tribological experiments were conducted on the top surface of the cold rolled (CR) UNS S32304. The lubricants used in these tests were distilled water and mineral oil, both at room temperature, selected to study the synergistic interaction between mechanical wear and the stability of the passive film in a corrosive environment. Disks (60 mm diameter, 5 mm thickness) were prepared by sequential grinding with SiC abrasive paper up to 1200 grit, followed by rinsing with distilled water, ultrasonic cleaning in ethanol, and drying. Tests were performed using a pin-on-disk tribometer with a 4.0 mm diameter alumina sphere as the counter-body. A constant normal load of 2.0 N (Hertzian contact stress ~ 1.23 GPa) was applied for one hour at a sliding speed corresponding to a 25 mm wear track diameter and 50 rpm rotational speed. The friction coefficient was recorded in situ via a load cell at 10 Hz sample frequency. Surface roughness was quantified before and after testing using a Mitutoyo SJ-210 profilometer, and wear track cross sections were profiled to determine volumetric wear. For comparative baseline assessment, identical tests were performed using mineral oil as the lubricant to isolate the effect of the aqueous corrosive medium on friction and wear response.

sections.heading: Microstructural Characterization
paragraphs: Figure  3  shows the calculated phase equilibrium of the UNS S32304 steel. Under equilibrium conditions, the alloy undergoes predominantly single-phase solidification, forming a body-centered cubic (ferrite) structure starting at approximately 1500 °C. As the temperature decreases and reaches a critical threshold, nucleation and growth of the face-centered cubic (austenite) structure begin within the ferritic matrix. This marks the onset of the two-phase coexistence in the material. The minimum temperature of the single-phase ferritic field is around 1250 °C. Therefore, below this temperature, the presence of a fraction of the austenite phase together with the ferritic matrix is expected. The transformation of the ferritic matrix into an approximately equal proportion of ferrite and austenite occurs at around 1100 °C, which corresponds to the temperature range used for a preliminary cold rolling before transversal cold rolling processing to ensure a balanced and banded duplex microstructure. Figure  3  (left) depicts a magnified region where the volume fraction plateaus at 0.0003. Fig. 3 Equilibrium solidification of UNS S32304 steel obtained using the CALPHAD method and the Thermo-Calc software with a commercial database for ferrous alloys (TCFE7)

From the Fe-Cu equilibrium phase diagram (Ref  32 ), it can be observed that at temperatures below 600 °C, the miscibility between these two elements is almost zero. Furthermore, these results are in good agreement with the positive mixing enthalpy of the Fe-Cu system, which has a value of approximately 13 kJ/mol, promoting the precipitation of copper within the iron matrix during solidification. Thus, there is a high probability that copper forms small and isolated precipitates during the cooling process, as shown in the left plot of Fig.  3 . Unfortunately, due to the overall very low concentration of copper, it is very difficult to detect these precipitates using the EDS technique, mainly because of the limitations of this method. On the other hand, Thermo-Calc simulations predict that these copper nanoparticles, if exist in this steel, would have a volume fraction below 0.0003.

Figure  4  shows synchrotron x-ray diffraction patterns for the HR and CR conditions. x-ray diffractograms indicate that only ferrite and austenite are present in the alloy under both conditions, meaning that no induced martensite phase or σ phase seem to be formed. After transverse cold rolling, the (110) peak becomes more intense, which is consistent with grain refinement resulting from deformation. The inset in Fig.  4  depicts the magnified patterns of the three most relevant peaks for both conditions. A noticeable difference in the full width at half maximum (FWHM) is observed between hot rolling and transverse cold rolling: peak broadening occurs after transverse cold rolling, evidence of grain refinement. Fig. 4 Indexed SXRD diffraction from each section of the UNS S32304 steel under HR and CR processing conditions

Figure  5  presents SEM-BSE images of the UNS S32304 alloy under HR condition, in both LS and TS. Both austenite (light gray) and ferrite (dark gray) are partially banded and aligned with the rolling direction. In both sections the microstructures reveal that the austenite phase is partially fragmented with an appearance of blocky shape. However, clear differences in aspect ratio (i.e., the relationship between width and height) of the austenite between the LS and TS are observed. In the LS micrograph, the lamellae appear highly elongated along rolling direction, exhibiting large lengths (10-80  µ m) and relatively small thicknesses (typically below ~ 10  µ m), indicating that deformation during cold rolling strongly stretched the phases in the longitudinal direction. In contrast, the TS micrograph shows lamellae with significantly lower aspect ratios since the same elongated features appear considerably shorter (10-30  µ m) and exhibit more equiaxed morphology. Although the hot-rolled UNS S32304 alloy microstructure is not fully stretched along the rolling direction, meaning that there is a morphological anisotropy in both LS and TS, this condition is more appropriate for the aims of this study than the IHR condition. This banded alignment can be modified by subsequent transverse cold rolling, which can contribute to improved isotropy of the material. Fig. 5 SEM-BSE images of UNS S32304 steel in HR condition are shown for the LS (top) and TS (bottom)

The volume fraction of the ferrite ( X α ) and austenite ( X γ ) phases in LS and TS of the UNS S32304 steel under HR and CR processing conditions is presented in Table  2 . The fraction values were estimated from the optical micrographs using the ImageJ image processing software. The difference in the amount of ferrite and austenite phases indicates that the hot rolling process, although carried out at the temperature predicted by CALPHAD calculation, was not sufficient to ensure proper balance of phases. The fraction values of the austenite phase in the TS and LS are maintained after transverse cold rolling, which may indicate that no strain-induced martensite is formed. Numerous studies on DSSs indicate that austenite transforms into deformation-induced martensite after conventional cold rolling processing, with the martensite fraction increasing as the degree of thickness reduction rises (Ref  33 ,  34 ). For example, Gonçalves et al. (Ref  35 ) show strain-induced martensite formation in the UNS S32304 steel after conventional cold rolling up to 62-64% thickness reduction. It is also reported that cold rolling up to 60% thickness reduction ( ε  = − 0.92) of the UNS S31803 steel results in only 2.8% of the austenite transforming into deformation-induced martensite. Considering that such true strain value is similar to that applied here (50% thickness reduction), it is also possible to consider that, if deformation-induced martensite was formed in the UNS S32304 steel under CR condition, its amount is likely to be very small, making its quantification by conventional metallography unreliable.

Figure  6  presents SEM-BSE images from both the LS and TS of the UNS S32304 steel under HR and CR conditions. Transverse cold rolling flattened and elongated the lamellae of austenite and ferrite phases in both sections. Also, in the LS from CR (the prior TS from HR) a wave pancake microstructure is formed due to the mechanical deformation incompatibility between ferrite and austenite. Wave pancake is also observed in the UNS S32304 steel when cold rolling up to 63% thickness reduction was applied in the same direction as the prior cold rolling (Ref  15 ). The steel investigated here shows no indication of deformation-induced martensite based on x-ray and metallographic characterization. All this together should help reduce anisotropy after transversal cold rolling. Fig. 6 SEM-BSE images from LS and TS of the UNS S32304 steel under HR and CR processing conditions. Magnification: 500 ×

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: The stress–strain curve for top section Top, LS, and TS under HR and CR conditions of the UNS S32304 steel is displayed in Fig.  7 . Table  3  presents the values for each of the properties and their standard deviations, as well as the results of Tukey’s post hoc test. The findings show an increase of approximately 73% in the UTS after CR, regardless of the analyzed section, and an increase of up to 60% in the  σ ys , depending on the section. For the same alloy conventionally cold rolled to a 30% thickness reduction, the longitudinal section exhibits  σ ys , UTS, and ε values of around 1035 MPa, 1048 MPa, and 1.4%, respectively (Ref  15 ). Comparable results were reported in a similar study on a 19 wt.% Cr duplex stainless steel after conventional cold rolling up to 40% and 60% thickness reductions (Ref  36 ). Although the different strain levels hinder a direct one-to-one comparison, the results suggest that cross rolling at 50% thickness reduction promotes a redistribution of strain and mechanical response, leading to lower yield strength and uniform elongation while maintaining a comparable ultimate tensile strength for the TS (former longitudinal section). This behavior indicates a modification of deformation accommodation mechanisms relative to conventional rolling at lower reductions. Further considering the values of these properties obtained in the present work for the UNS S32304 steel (0.01% C), they exceeded those observed in low carbon steel processed by asymmetric cold rolling up to 75% thickness reduction (Ref  37 ), but remain lower than those reported for ODS duplex stainless steel processed by multistep cross rolling up to 65% thickness reduction (Ref  20 ). The ductility behavior is very similar for all sections after cold rolling the UNS S32304 steel, indicating that only the  σ ys  exhibits a section-dependent property. Previous studies have shown that cross cold rolling up to 40% in austenitic stainless steel reduces considerably anisotropy (Ref  19 ). Asymmetric cold deformation up to 75% in low carbon steel leads to a decrease in anisotropy due to the weakening of the gamma fiber texture (Ref  37 ). Although the reduction in anisotropy observed here was not as significant as that reported in these studies, the transverse cold rolling route implemented in this study contributed to reducing the anisotropic behavior relative to the solely deformed the UNS S32304 steel. A crystallographic texture study is required to provide further insight into the origin of this variation (Ref  38 ).

The microhardness of each section of the UNS S32304 steel under HR and CR conditions is presented in Fig.  8 . The microhardness increases by up to 40% depending on the section. Conversely, the increase in hardness, UTS and  σ ys  in the TS after transverse cold rolling is attributed to the work hardening, although this increase in hardness is not strongly pronounced. The UNS S32304 and lean duplex stainless steels, when conventionally cold rolled (Ref  39 ,  40 ), exhibits comparable Vickers microhardness values in the longitudinal section when compared with the values obtained here for transverse cold rolling. Previous studies have reported that, compared to conventional rolling, cross rolling promotes the transformation of the austenite phase from a striped to a granular morphology, enhancing ferrite continuity and enabling the ferrite phase to accommodate higher strains, thereby improving deformation uniformity and material processability (Ref  21 ). Thus, considering the observed micrographs and the mechanical property results, it can be inferred that transverse cold rolling, that is, a single 90° rotation step followed by multiple deformation passes in the same direction up to 50% thickness reduction, was not sufficient to fragment all the austenite in UNS S32304 steel to ensure a fully continuous ferritic network. As a result, the material did not achieve optimal deformation accommodation, especially by ferrite phase, leading to a less uniform distribution of properties throughout the different sections. Despite the partial mechanical constraint imposed by the ferrite together with the low Mn content, the lack of evidence for the presence of deformation-induced martensite in the transverse cold rolled UNS S32304 steel may be attributed to the high intrinsic stability of the austenite phase due to 22.7 Cr, 4.5 Ni and 0.08 wt.% N additions (Ref  41 ,  42 ). Fig. 8 Vickers microhardness measurements of the TOP, LS and TS of the UNS S32304 steel under HR and CR conditions. Different letters (a, b, c) indicate statistically significant differences according to Tukey’s post hoc test ( α  = 0.01), where identical letters represent no significant difference among conditions

sections.heading: Corrosion Behavior
paragraphs: Anodic cyclic polarization tests were used to evaluate the corrosion behavior of the top section of UNS S32304 steel subjected to IHR, HR, and CR processing conditions (Fig.  9 ). The electrochemical behavior observed in the anodic polarization curves can be directly correlated with the microstructural features developed during thermomechanical processing. All conditions exhibit similar corrosion potentials, with  E corr  close to − 0.10  V SCE , and similar curves at small anodic cyclic polarization, indicating comparable initial electrochemical stability. A well-defined passive region is observed for all conditions, characterized by a passive current density of approximately 3  µ A cm −2 . The IHR condition exhibits the highest pitting potential, around 0.80-0.85  V SCE , followed by the CR condition (~0.65-0.70  V SCE ) and the HR condition (~0.55-0.60  V SCE ). In addition, the IHR sample shows a higher protection potential indicating greater stability of the passive film and enhanced repassivation capability. In contrast, the HR condition presents a lower protection potential, consistent with a more heterogeneous microstructure. In this case, the microstructure probably consists of deformed, recrystallized, and recovered grains, exhibiting both equiaxed and elongated morphologies and thus a higher density of preferential sites for pit initiation. Although the CR condition introduces additional plastic deformation (Ref  36 ,  39 ), and considering that the volume fraction of austenite is similar for both HR and CR conditions but higher than in IHR condition, the associated microstructural refinement and improved phase distribution allow the material to maintain passive current densities and protection potentials comparable to those of the IHR condition, despite a slight reduction in pitting potential. The results confirm that the probable microstructural homogeneity generated by transverse cold rolling appears to influence the control of the localized corrosion resistance of UNS S32304 alloy in the chloride environment. Fig. 9 Cyclic polarization curves of the top section of the UNS S32304 steel under all processing conditions

Table  4  presents the electrochemical parameters derived from the cyclic potentiodynamic polarization scans (Fig.  9 ). These measurements were recorded at a scan rate of 1.0 mV/s, with the potential sweep reversed once the anodic current density reached a threshold of 10 mA/cm 2 . The corrosion potential ( E corr ) of the IHR Top sample is 40 mV higher than those of the CR Top and HR Top samples. However, for passive alloys, this small shift in corrosion potential is less significant than the pitting potential ( E pit ), which provides a more critical measure of the resistance of passive film to localized attack by chloride. IHR Top sample has a higher resistance to pitting, followed by CR Top and the worst was the HR Top. Consistently, the passive range (Δ E pass ), measured between the pitting potential ( E pit ) and the potential at which anodic activity returns to the passivation current density ( i pass ), is wider for the IHR Top sample. Here, this positive behavior is primarily attributed to a more noble  E pit  and a more positive repassivation potential ( E rep ). At potentials below  E rep , the anodic current decays as existing pits cease to propagate and the passive film is restored; however, the pit cavity remains on metallic surface.

The degradation in passive film stability in CR specimens aligns with studies on cold worked duplex stainless steel of Chen et al. (Ref  41 ) and Li et al. (Ref  43 ). They demonstrated that severe plastic deformation induces strain-induced martensite and dislocation networks, which disrupt the continuity of the passive film. These defects act as preferential sites for chloride ion adsorption, accelerating pit initiation, a phenomenon corroborated by the steeper anodic slopes in the CR polarization curves. Furthermore, Yang et al. (Ref  44 ) showed that in cold worked 2205 duplex stainless steel, residual stresses and strain partitioning between ferrite and austenite promote pitting initiation preferentially within the austenite and at  α / γ  interfaces, highlighting the role of micro-galvanic coupling in localized corrosion.

Wang et al. (Ref  45 ) linked this result to the segregation of alloying elements (e.g., Mo, Cr) at phase boundaries during cold rolling. Such segregation reduces the effective Cr content in the matrix adjacent to grain boundaries, impairing repassivation capacity. This mechanism is critical in chloride-rich environments, where the breakdown of Cr-depleted zones leads to sustained active dissolution. Khoshnaw et al. (Ref  46 ) further highlighted that cold rolling without subsequent annealing promotes the formation of metastable pits, which evolve into stable pits due to insufficient repassivation kinetics.

The double-loop electrochemical potentiokinetic reactivation (DL-EPR) curves shown in Fig.  10  reveal distinct sensitization trends across the Top, Longitudinal and Transversal sections of UNS S32304 of IHR, HR and CR conditions. The observed behavior indicates accelerated dissolution kinetics and reduced stability of the passive film in this medium, consistent with the degree of sensitization (DOS) observed via DL-EPR. Although the carbon content is low, thermomechanical processing may increase local sensitization. According to ISO 12372 (Ref  31 ), an  I r / I a  ratio below 1% signifies unsensitized material, 1-5% denotes slight sensitization, and above 5% indicates severe sensitization. Fig. 10 DL-EPR curves and the degree of sensitization, Ir/Ia (%) of each section: (a) Top, (b) Longitudinal, (c) Transversal, and the general interpretation according to the ISO 12372 standard

In the Top section, the IHR specimens displays negligible reactivation peaks ( I r / I a  < 1%), indicating an unsensitized condition and a microstructure free of significant chromium-depleted regions. After cold rolling, a slight increase in  I r / I a  is observed, although values remain below 1%, suggesting that deformation-induced defects do not significantly promote chromium depletion under the present conditions. The CR condition exhibits a similar response, with I r /I a  values still within the unsensitized regime. This indicates that cold deformation alone is insufficient to induce classical sensitization in the absence of thermal exposure capable of promoting carbide or intermetallic precipitation. The LS direction follows comparable behavior, although slightly higher  I r / I a  values are observed. The IHR conditions remain unsensitized, while HR and CR conditions show a modest increase in reactivation current. Notably, the CR LS  sample exhibits the highest  I r / I a  value (~ 3.5%), corresponding to a slightly sensitized condition according to ISO 12732. This behavior suggests that the combination of deformation and crystallographic orientation may locally enhance chromium redistribution or promote the formation of incipient chromium-depleted regions.

In the TS section, all conditions remain within the unsensitized range, despite negligible variations in  I r / I a . The absence of significant reactivation peaks indicates that deformation-induced defects, such as increased dislocation density and strain localization, do not result in sufficient chromium depletion to trigger intergranular corrosion susceptibility. Overall, the DL-EPR results demonstrate that, although cold rolling introduces microstructural heterogeneities and increases defect density, it does not lead to significant sensitization in the study lean duplex stainless steel.

Comparatively, the HR and IHR conditions retained a stable passive region, underscoring the importance of balanced phase proportions and minimal lattice defects. The work of Wang et al. (Ref  47 ) supports this observation, showing that hot-rolled DSS with equiaxed  α / γ  microstructures exhibit superior passive film integrity due to homogeneous elemental distribution and lower dislocation density.

To mitigate the corrosion drawbacks of cold rolling, recent advancements propose hybrid processing routes. For instance, short-duration annealing after cold rolling promotes recovery and recrystallization, leading to a reduction in strain-induced defects and dislocation density, which in turn facilitates chromium diffusion and improves the chemical quality of the passive film, resulting in a recovery of passivity and corrosion resistance. Implementing such strategies could reconcile the mechanical benefits of cold rolling with the electrochemical stability required for harsh environments, such as marine or chemical processing applications.

sections.heading: Tribological Behavior
paragraphs: Figure  11  shows the coefficient of friction as a function of time (COF vs. time) obtained from pin-on-disk wear test of UNS S32304 steel in the CR condition conducted in distilled water (H 2 O) and mineral oil. The COF values stabilize only after approximately 1200 s, corresponding to the time required for the passive film to be mechanically worn to a steady-state condition. Once this barrier is disrupted, the COF values remain relatively constant. Accordingly, the representative COF was calculated as the arithmetic means of the data in the stabilized interval between 1200 and 3600 s. Thus, the COF values, including measurement uncertainties, are 0.66 ± 0.07 for H 2 O and 0.12 ± 0.02 for mineral oil, respectively. Throughout the entire test in the H 2 O medium, pronounced COF fluctuations are observed, indicating an unstable tribological regime dominated by boundary or near dry lubrification conditions. This behavior suggests frequent metal–metal contact, associated with repeated formation and disruption of oxide layers on the UNS S32304 steel surface. The sustained high COF values and their variability likely reflect progressive surface degradation and increase surface roughness. In contrast, tests conducted in mineral oil exhibit a short running-in period, followed by stabilization at low COF values, and remain relatively constant over time with only minor fluctuations. This response indicates a stable and efficient lubricated regime, associated with the formation and maintenance of a continuous lubricant film that effectively separates the contacting surfaces and minimizes direct asperity interaction (Ref  48 ). As a result, the UNS S32304 steel exhibits reduced friction and a lower tendency for wear, highlighting the effectiveness of oil lubrication in promoting favorable tribological performance. Fig. 11 Coefficient of friction (COF) curves as a function of time for the transversal cold rolled UNS S32304 steel tested under different lubricating conditions: oil and water

Figure  12  shows the wear track depth profiles as a function of track width for the UNS S32304 steel under the CR condition, tested in distilled water and mineral oil. The wear rates calculated from the test parameters are 8061  μ m 3  N −1  m −1  in the H 2 O medium and 36257  μ m 3  N −1  m −1  in mineral oil. Under water-lubricated conditions, the wear profile is relatively shallow and homogeneous, with small depth variations across the transverse section, indicating a milder and more controlled wear regime. This behavior is consistent with the ability of stainless steel to form and continuously regenerate a chromium oxide-rich passive film in the presence of oxygen, which effectively limits material removal. In contrast, the test conducted in mineral oil exhibits a deeper and more irregular wear profile, characterized by pronounced peaks and valleys, indicating greater material loss and the activation of more severe wear mechanisms. Despite the lower coefficient of friction measured in this medium, the increased wear depth suggests that the absence of oxygen inhibits rapid surface repassivation after mechanical rupture of the passive film, as previously reported by Shima et al. (Ref  49 ). Additionally, the retention of wear debris within the contact zone due to the high viscosity of the oil promotes three-body abrasion, further contributing to the higher wear rate observed, in agreement with the discussed by Chen and Horng (Ref  50 ). Fig. 12 Cross sectional wear track profiles of UNS S32304 steel after pin-on-disk tests performed in distilled water and mineral oil

Although the mineral oil medium exhibits a significantly lower coefficient of friction than distilled water, it results in a markedly higher wear rate, highlighting that friction and wear are not necessarily correlated. In the oil-lubricated condition, the absence of oxygen suppresses the rapid reformation of the chromium oxide-rich passive film after mechanical disruption, preventing effective surface healing and allowing cumulative material removal. In contrast, under water-lubricated conditions, repeated breakdown and reformation of the passive film promote a self-limiting wear mechanism, leading to shallower and more homogeneous wear tracks despite higher friction levels. This decoupling between friction and wear is further exacerbated by the high viscosity of the mineral oil, which favors the entrapment of wear debris within the contact zone, promoting three-body abrasion and localized stress concentrations that accelerate material loss. Besides, at low sliding speeds, oil film formation is hindered, resulting in poor lubrification conditions (Ref  51 ).

The observed wear behavior is also influenced by the microstructural state produced by transverse cold rolling. Although cold rolling increases hardness through work hardening, the hardening response is heterogeneous due to the partially fragmented and anisotropic duplex microstructure, in which ferrite and austenite accommodate strain differently. The incomplete fragmentation of austenite and the lack of a fully continuous ferritic network limit the ability of the ferrite phase to uniformly support the applied load, leading to localized plastic deformation and preferential wear in mechanically weaker regions. As a result, the moderate hardness increase achieved after transverse cold rolling is insufficient to counteract the severe wear mechanisms activated under oxygen-depleted lubrication. These findings indicate that wear resistance in UNS S32304 steel is governed not only by bulk hardness but also by the interplay between microstructural anisotropy, deformation accommodation between phases, and tribochemical surface reactions.

Collectively, the electrochemical and tribological results highlight the critical role of passive film stability and regeneration in determining the surface performance of UNS S32304 steel under various service conditions. While anodic cyclic polarization and DL-EPR analyses reveal that thermomechanical processing, particularly transverse cold rolling, modifies localized corrosion susceptibility through increased defect density and sensitization, the tribological results demonstrate that the same passive film critically influences friction and wear behavior. In aqueous environments, the ability to continuously reform a Cr-rich oxide layer mitigates material loss despite elevated friction and unstable sliding, linking corrosion passivity to wear resistance. Conversely, under oil lubrication, the absence of oxygen limits repassivation, decoupling low friction from wear protection and resulting in deeper wear tracks despite favorable COF values. These findings indicate that cold work-induced microstructural heterogeneities affect both electrochemical and tribological responses through a shared mechanism involving passive film integrity, rupture, and renewal. Consequently, the surface durability of duplex stainless steels cannot be assessed by corrosion or tribology independently, but rather must be interpreted through their coupled interaction, particularly in environments where mechanical and electrochemical processes act simultaneously.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The effect of transverse cold rolling up to 50% thickness reduction on microstructure, and mechanical and corrosion properties of UNS S32304 lean duplex stainless steel were investigated. The following conclusions were drawn from this study: Transverse cold rolling with a 50% thickness reduction partially modifies, but does not eliminate, the original banded alignment of the hot-rolled UNS S32304 steel. Microstructural observations and mechanical results indicate that anisotropy is retained after processing. Although transverse cold rolling increases the yield strength by up to 60% depending on the analyzed section, increases the ultimate tensile stress by up to 73% regardless of the section, and increases the microhardness by up to 40% in the longitudinal section. This approach neither triggers deformation-induced martensitic transformation, nor ensures a strongly isotropic mechanical response. Electrochemical cyclic potentiodynamic polarization test conducted in aqueous 3.5% NaCl at 25 °C reveals, for the top section, a passive behavior with an average passive current density of 4  µ A cm −2 . The hot and transverse cold rolling processes applied after industrial hot rolling and annealed UNS S32304 steel reduce the pitting potential by approximately 0.2 V in relation to the initial industrially processed condition. Despite the good corrosion resistance of UNS S32304, the steel exhibits relatively poor tribological performance in distilled water. However, the experimental results show that the wear severity in distilled water is lower than that observed in the mineral oil medium.
